newsitem.title: USA: Midnight strike deadline looms at United Parcel Service.
newsitem.headline: Midnight strike deadline looms at United Parcel Service.

text.p: Only hours before a Teamsters strike threatened to shut down United Parcel Service -- paralysing 12 million packages a day -- labour and management were deadlocked and no longer talking.
The director of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, John Calhoun Wells, was talking to both sides "to arrange appropriate meetings," a spokesman for the service said.
The White House talked to both sides but made no move to intervene in the strike.

The company made its "last, best and final offer" Wednesday evening, United Parcel Service spokesman Ken Sternad said from company headquarters in Atlanta. The union rejected that offer Thursday and said the company was refusing to talk.

"UPS claims to have made a final offer," said Ken Hall, co-chairman of the Teamsters' National Negotiating Committee in Washington. "The fact is, the last offer that UPS has put on the table does not address all the serious issues and the serious proposals that we have put on the table."

At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry said a senior adviser, Bruce Lindsey, had met with officials from both the United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union. But McCurry declined to speculate about intervention.
"I'm not going to speculate on that at this point. We've just had contact with the parties to understand better their deliberations," he said.

President Clinton lacks authority to halt a UPS drivers strike in the way he ended a brief strike by American Airlines pilots earlier this year under the Railway Labour Act. Instead, he would have to invoke the more cumbersome and far-more time-consuming Taft-Hartley law.
If the strike takes place, Congress might be inclined to reconsider labour laws governing UPS, an analyst said.
The strike would put approximately 200,000 Teamsters out of work. The two sides even disagreed on that number: The union said 185,000 and the company 214,000.

One key issue was the fate of part-timers at UPS. More than half of all union members have part-time jobs. The company has offered to convert roughly one in 10 of the part-time employees -- 10,000 of them -- to full-time work over the five-year contract. The union says that is not enough.
The company also wants to break up the Teamsters pension fund, substituting a joint company-union pension fund that includes only UPS employees.
"We believe UPS dollars should directly benefit UPS employees, not support the Teamsters' pension funds," company spokesman Sternad said.
The company says that would improve pension benefits and might help it financially, as well.
"We anticipate in the long run there could be savings to UPS," Sternad said.
A union spokesman declined to respond.

"We are not going to negotiate this in the media," said Rand Wilson. But a union negotiator, who asked not to be identified, said if the company took over the pension plan, employees would be unable to switch companies and preserve their pensions.
The contract would increase top pay for full-time workers from $19.95 an hour to $21.45 by 2001 -- which the company says would be the highest in the industry.
The lowest paid part-time employees, who now earn $8 an hour, would get $11 an hour by 2001.
The union also objects to the use of subcontractors instead of union help. The company says that only a small percentage of its business is handled that way, but the union says it is more.
If the strike does take place, the company's roughly 2,000 pilots -- who operate its 200 aircraft -- pledged to honour the picket line and not fly.

The company is the largest package carrier in the country, with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
